name.en: The Tel Dan Stele ('House of David')

modernLocation.en: Israel Museum, Jerusalem (found at Tel Dan, 1993-94)

corroborates.en: An Aramaic victory stele whose 'BYTDWD' is read by most scholars as 'House of David' — the earliest extra-biblical reference to the Davidic dynasty, c. 9th c. BC. A minority contest the reading.

modernLocation.en: Louvre, Paris (found at Dhiban, Jordan, 1868)

corroborates.en: King Mesha of Moab's inscription (c. 840 BC) recounting revolt against Israel; it names Omri king of Israel, YHWH, and the town of Nebo — paralleling 2 Kings 3. Some read a damaged line as 'House of David'.

modernLocation.en: Egyptian Museum, Cairo (found at Thebes, 1896)

corroborates.en: Pharaoh Merneptah's victory stele (c. 1208 BC) carries the earliest known mention of 'Israel' as a people in Canaan — a fixed point for Israel's presence in the land by the late 13th c. BC.

modernLocation.en: Excavated near the Church of St Anne, Old City of Jerusalem

corroborates.en: A twin-pool complex with five porticoes matching John 5:2 — long doubted until excavation confirmed its form, a case where topographical detail in John was archaeologically vindicated.

name.en: The House of St Peter, Capernaum

modernLocation.en: Capernaum, on the Sea of Galilee (beneath the modern memorial church)

corroborates.en: A 1st-c. house singled out very early for veneration (graffiti, later octagonal church) and identified by tradition as Peter's house, where Jesus stayed and healed (Mark 1:29-31). The identification is traditional.

name.en: Hezekiah's Tunnel and the Siloam Inscription

modernLocation.en: Tunnel in the City of David; inscription in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums

corroborates.en: An 8th-c. BC water tunnel and its paleo-Hebrew inscription recording the diggers' meeting — matching Hezekiah's works before Sennacherib's siege (2 Kings 20:20; 2 Chronicles 32:30). It belongs with the earlier Siloam dam (exposed 2025; radiocarbon c. 805–795 BC, Joash and Amaziah): two generations of Judah's kings shaping the same spring-and-pool system the Gospels later name.

name.en: Siloam dam of Joash and Amaziah (2025)

modernLocation.en: Southern mouth of the Tyropoeon Valley, City of David / Pool of Siloam, Jerusalem

corroborates.en: The largest dam yet found in ancient Israel: about 12 m high, 8 m wide, 21 m of length exposed. IAA excavators (Szanton, Berko, Vukosavović) and Weizmann radiocarbon (Regev, Boaretto and colleagues, 2025) date its construction to c. 805–795 BC, the reigns of Joash and Amaziah of Judah (2 Kings 12–14). It impounded Gihon overflow and valley runoff to form the earliest Pool of Siloam — the same water system Hezekiah later tunnelled, and the pool John 9 names.

modernLocation.en: Copies in the British Museum, Oriental Institute (Chicago), and Israel Museum

corroborates.en: Sennacherib's own account of his 701 BC campaign says he shut up Hezekiah 'like a bird in a cage' in Jerusalem — corroborating the siege of 2 Kings 18-19 while, tellingly, never claiming to take the city.

modernLocation.en: Found in the Ophel excavations, City of David, Jerusalem (2015)

corroborates.en: A clay seal impression reading 'Belonging to Hezekiah [son of] Ahaz, king of Judah' — a royal artifact naming a biblical king of Judah, from controlled excavation.

modernLocation.en: British Museum, London (found at Babylon, 1879)

corroborates.en: Cyrus the Great's proclamation (c. 539 BC) of restoring displaced peoples and their sanctuaries — the imperial policy behind the return from exile and the temple's rebuilding (Ezra 1; 6). Its direct bearing on Judah is inferred, not named.

modernLocation.en: Inscriptions from Cyprus, Pisidian Antioch, and Rome

corroborates.en: Several inscriptions attest the aristocratic Sergii Pauli family, consistent with the proconsul Sergius Paulus whom Paul met on Cyprus (Acts 13:7); which individual Luke names is debated.

disputes.en: Inscriptions confirm the family and its standing, but securely matching a specific attested Sergius Paulus to Luke's Cypriot proconsul is not possible; the identification is probable, not certain.

modernLocation.en: Yigal Allon Museum, Kibbutz Ginosar, Sea of Galilee (found 1986)

corroborates.en: A 1st-century wooden fishing boat (~8.8 m long) uncovered in the lakebed mud between Ginosar and Magdala during a 1986 drought by brothers Moshe and Yuval Lufan. Radiocarbon dating, pottery, and nail analysis place its use c. 50 BC–AD 50 — the kind of vessel the Gospels describe Jesus and his fishermen disciples using on the Sea of Galilee (Matthew 8:23-27; Mark 4:35-41; Luke 5:1-11).

modernLocation.en: British Museum, London (BM 21946); excavated at Babylon

corroborates.en: A Neo-Babylonian scribal tablet recording that in Nebuchadnezzar’s 7th year (597 BC) his army besieged and took the ‘city of Judah’ (Jerusalem), captured its king (Jehoiachin/Jeconiah), appointed a king of his choosing (Zedekiah), and took tribute to Babylon — matching the account in 2 Kings 24:10-17, 2 Chronicles 36:9-10, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel.

name.en: Durupınar formation surveys — GPR scans (2019) and soil analyses (2022–2024)

modernLocation.en: Durupınar site, near Üzengili, Doğubayazıt district, Ağrı Province, Türkiye — GPS 39.4406° N, 44.2347° E

corroborates.en: A boat-shaped formation about 160 m (538 ft) long, on the flank of Mount Tendürek, its outline loosely echoing the ark's 300 cubits (Genesis 6:15). The independent Noah's Ark Scans team (led by Andrew Jones) reports that ground-penetrating-radar surveys from 2019 onward show linear, right-angled reflectors — with later re-analysis describing angular features to about 6 m depth, three stacked layers read as decks, and a ~13 m central corridor — and that soil samples from 22 points (2022–2024) hold roughly double the organic matter inside the formation versus outside, with pH and potassium shifts the team reads as consistent with decayed wood. Advocates present these as a buried, decayed wooden vessel.

disputes.en: None of these survey results are peer-reviewed or independently replicated. A 1960 archaeological dig at the site turned up only soil and rock, and mainstream geologists (Collins & Fasold 1996) identify the formation as a doubly plunging syncline — a natural structure whose 'boat ribs' are concentrations of limonite and magnetite in steeply inclined sedimentary beds — with no petrified wood present. Shown as a documented claim, not an established find.

modernLocation.en: Tell Fara, southern Iraq

corroborates.en: Excavations at Shuruppak — and at Kish and Ur — exposed river-flood silt strata from around the Jemdet Nasr / Early Dynastic transition (c. 2900 BC). That is the same window as the biblical Flood (Ussher: 2348 BC, from the Genesis 5 intervals): catastrophic flooding on the same plain, complementary as the material setting of Genesis 6-9, not a second clock.

disputes.en: Archaeologists read the silts at the several cities as local river floods of more than one episode, not as a single universal deluge, and the ceramic date (~2900 BC) is not a synchronism that locks Ussher's 2348 BC. Shown as complementary setting — the same plain, the same age — not as a year-lock.

modernLocation.en: British Museum, London (from Sennacherib's 'Palace Without Rival', Nineveh)

corroborates.en: Sennacherib's own wall-carvings of the 701 BC storming of Lachish — siege ramp, battering rams, archers, impaled defenders, and files of Judean deportees — matching 2 Kings 18:13-14 ('Sennacherib... came up against all the fenced cities of Judah, and took them') and the ramp, arrowheads, and burn layer excavated at the tell itself. The fullest visual record of any event named in the Bible.

modernLocation.en: British Museum, London, and the Israel Museum, Jerusalem

corroborates.en: Eighteen ink-on-sherd military dispatches found in the burned gate-room of Lachish, written as Nebuchadnezzar's army reduced Judah c. 589-588 BC. Letter IV reports 'we are watching for the signals of Lachish... for we cannot see Azekah' — the same last-two-fortresses moment as Jeremiah 34:7.

name.en: The Kurkh Monolith of Shalmaneser III

modernLocation.en: British Museum, London (found at Kurkh, upper Tigris)

corroborates.en: Assyrian victory stele naming 'Ahab the Israelite' (A-ha-ab-bu mat Sir-'i-la-a-a) fielding 2,000 chariots and 10,000 soldiers in the coalition that met Shalmaneser III at Qarqar in 853 BC — the earliest securely dated extra-biblical mention of a king of Israel, and the synchronism that anchors the divided-kingdom chronology.

name.en: The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III

modernLocation.en: British Museum, London (found at Nimrud/Kalhu)

corroborates.en: Four-sided basalt obelisk whose second register shows 'Jehu son of Omri' (Ia-u-a mar Hu-um-ri) bowing to the ground before Shalmaneser III and rendering tribute in 841 BC — the only surviving ancient depiction of an Israelite king, within months of the coup of 2 Kings 9-10.

name.en: Khirbet Qeiyafa — the Elah fortress and ostracon

modernLocation.en: Khirbet Qeiyafa, above the Valley of Elah; ostracon in the Israel Museum

corroborates.en: A massively fortified, single-period city overlooking the Elah valley, radiocarbon-dated to c. 1020-980 BC, with a casemate wall, two gates (suggesting biblical Shaaraim, 1 Samuel 17:52), an absence of pig bones, and the earliest known Hebrew-language ostracon. Bears directly on whether a centralized kingdom existed in Judah in David's generation — the very valley of the Goliath duel.

disputes.en: Identification and ethnicity are argued: Garfinkel reads a Judahite fortress of David's kingdom; others propose a northern-Israelite, Philistine, or Canaanite town, and the 'Shaaraim' reading of the two gates is contested. The radiocarbon dating window itself is broadly accepted.

modernLocation.en: Pergamon Museum, Berlin (from the South Palace archive, Babylon)

corroborates.en: Babylonian administrative tablets (c. 592 BC) listing oil rations for 'Ya'u-kinu, king of the land of Yahudu' and his five sons — the exiled Jehoiachin of 2 Kings 24:15, held in Babylon exactly as 2 Kings 25:27-30 describes his maintenance at the royal table.

modernLocation.en: Found in the palace treasury quarter of Samaria; Istanbul Archaeology Museums

corroborates.en: Over a hundred eighth-century BC ink-inscribed sherds recording wine and oil shipments to the capital, written in the northern Hebrew dialect. Their clan and district names — Abiezer, Helek, Shechem, Shemida — match the Manassite clan lists of Joshua 17, fixing the tribal geography in the kingdom of Israel's own administration.

name.en: The fallen walls of Jericho (Tell es-Sultan)

modernLocation.en: Tell es-Sultan, Jericho — excavated ramparts in situ

corroborates.en: Collapsed mudbrick city walls lying at the base of the stone revetment — in places forming a ready ramp up into the city — with a thick destruction-burn layer and jars still full of charred grain from a short siege in spring, matching the sequence of Joshua 6 (walls fallen flat, city burned, harvest-time, plunder banned).

display.en: destruction c. 1550 BC (Kenyon) or c. 1400 BC (Garstang/Wood)

disputes.en: Kenyon dated the fallen City IV walls to c. 1550 BC (too early for any conquest chronology); Garstang and later Wood re-date the same destruction to c. 1400 BC on pottery and scarab grounds, matching the early conquest date. Bienkowski, Sharon and others defend Kenyon. The debate is unresolved and turns on Cypriot pottery and radiocarbon calibration.

name.en: The Late Bronze destruction of Hazor

modernLocation.en: Tel Hazor — excavated palace destruction in situ

corroborates.en: A violent, city-wide destruction ending Late Bronze Hazor (stratum XIII/1A, 13th century BC): the ceremonial palace burned at temperatures over 1,000 °C, and the heads and hands of Canaanite cult statues were deliberately severed — matching 'he burnt Hazor with fire' and the iconoclasm of Joshua 11:11-13. Who set the fire is argued; that the greatest city of Canaan fell exactly as only this one city is said to have been burned is the point of contact.
